newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FORECAST-Bank of Ireland sees steady growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Bank of Ireland sees steady growth.

text.p: Bank of Ireland Plc is expected to show steady growth at the half year mark when it reports results on Thursday, with its main retail market, Ireland, continuing to contribute the bulk of its profits.
Analysts are forecasting pre-tax profit for the six months to September of between 190 to 194 million punts compared with 191.8 million for the first half in 1995.
"I am going for a pre-tax profit of 192 million punts, a net dividend of 6.1 pence per share and earnings per share (EPS) of 24.7 pence," Goodbody stockbrokers analyst Oliver O'Shea said.

Riada's head of research John Hogan is expecting a full-year pre-tax outturn of 388 million punts and 51 pence EPS and is expecting profits to be relatively evenly split between the first and second half.
"The year will break down roughly half and half," Hogan said. "Pre-tax will be a bit higher and EPS a fraction lower but you have a slightly higher tax charge this time in the U.S."
He said BOI's U.S. operation had tax-free profits last year, being offset by accumulated losses, but as it was now part of Citizens Finanical Group its U.S. profits were taxable.

Ireland's banking sector is dominated by two main banks, Allied Irish Banks (AIB) and Bank of Ireland (BOI). They have, in the past, spread their eggs relatively similarly between Ireland, the UK and the U.S.
BOI broke this trend over the past year in two swift moves. Firstly it merged its U.S. operation First Holdings with Royal Bank of Scotland's Citizens Financial Group in December 1995.
The terms of the merger valued the enlarged bank at an estimated $1.85 billion with joint assets in excess of $14 billion. BOI has a 23.5 percent interest in Citizens valued at $435 million.
The second move came in April 1996 when Bank of Ireland announced it was acquiring British building society Bristol & West for 600 million sterling.
When BOI's Bristol & West acquisition comes on stream it will effectively have shifted a considerable number of its eggs to the UK basket and reduced its dependence on the U.S.

"At the moment 60 percent of BOI's business comes from Ireland, 19 percent from the UK," Riada's Hogan said. "If you take it that the Bristol and West deal is done by mid-1997 then BOI's UK interests will account about one third of its business, its dependence on Ireland will reduce to about 56 percent and the U.S. will account for 11 percent of business."
This compares to AIB spread of risk which is 49 percent Ireland, 22 percent UK and 29 percent U.S.
Hogan gives BOI's move his vote of confidence.

"The UK housing market appears to be picking up so the timing (of the Bristol & West buy) looks to be good," he said. "Ireland is doing quite well as you have strong growth in domestic lending. So the Ireland situation should be relatively buoyant as should the fund management operation as you have got strong markets and higher values," Hogan said.

At the half year stage Goodbody's O'Shea is expecting Ireland and the UK to account for 98.5 million punts of BOI's profits, on a grossed up basis. He expects the Corporate and Treasury operation, also based in Ireland, to contribute 36 million and associates, which includes the Bank's U.S. interest, to generate 20 million.
